source.title: Theoretical characterisation of the Gauss-Newton conditioning in Neural Networks
source.authors: Jim Zhao; Sidak Pal Singh; Aurélien Lucchi

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes Gauss-Newton conditioning and reports related training-loss results, but does not test the training-error behaviors specified in V1–V6. Its own reported measures are conditioning and training loss, not training classification error, convergence speed with batch normalization, or the other version-specific outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss plots for sparse networks trained from scratch and for networks of different widths, plus a three-seed training-loss trajectory. These results bear on related training behavior but do not measure the classification-error outcomes named in the versions. Conditioning measurements and cited results are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports Gauss–Newton conditioning and training-loss trajectories, but none measures a version's specified effect. Pruning slowdown does not establish training classification error; width-dependent convergence on MNIST does not measure teacher–student spurious minima; residual and batch-normalization comparisons measure conditioning at initialization rather than training performance. Initialization bounds do not compare learning speed or trainable depth, and no experiment tests learning-rate stability thresholds.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors derive Gauss–Newton condition-number bounds, show how data conditioning, depth, width, and residual connections affect conditioning in linear networks, and empirically find improved conditioning with batch normalization and with ReLU relative to linear activation in the tested one-hidden-layer setting. They explicitly acknowledge that their bounds are agnostic to training dynamics and cannot distinguish initialization from converged solutions.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes Gauss-Newton conditioning theoretically and empirically; its training experiments use SGD to track loss or conditioning, rather than testing the claim versions' training-classification-error outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported conditioning and training behavior varies with pruning rate and width; the paper also reports conditioning differences with depth, residual connections, data whitening, and activation choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning weights by magnitude at initialization slows the reported ResNet20 training-loss decline on a 1,000-image CIFAR-10 subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning at initialization can slow optimization in the tested training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: The three-layer linear network's Gauss–Newton condition number remains between 6 and 12 during training, and the derived upper bound remains tight.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial Gauss–Newton conditioning can be indicative of conditioning throughout training in this linear-network setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider one-hidden-layer ReLU networks show faster training-loss convergence on the MNIST subset under the width-specific learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Greater hidden width is associated with faster convergence under the tested recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth, width, residual connections, data whitening, activation choice, and batch normalization affect Gauss–Newton conditioning; the batch-normalization comparison measures conditioning at initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural and data-normalization choices affect Gauss–Newton conditioning in the analyzed settings.

record.problems: The relevant training-loss results are shown in figures without textual numeric values; the study does not report classification error for these experiments. The reported loss trajectory is for a three-layer linear network, not the non-convex classification settings in the versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and qualifications involving size, early stopping, or regularization.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies in realizable two-layer ReLU teacher–student problems and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Depth-dependent training-error degradation in plain convolutional networks, its prevention by identity shortcuts, and the special-initialization and Fixup comparisons.
Effects of activation-matched initialization on learning speed and trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian learning speed, and training 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Loss recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to stability thresholds.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy-gain speed and tolerated learning rates, and comparable training speed and stability with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Conditioning results are related evidence, but they do not establish the training outcomes named by V1–V6. The additional pruning experiments likewise report loss and conditioning rather than those version-specific outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; comparisons involving model size, early stopping, or regularized recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious minima, and the effect of student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual batch-normalized convolutional networks' training error as depth increases, and the stated special-initialization or normalization-free residual comparisons.
Whether initialization choices change training speed or trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Training dynamics above or near a learning-rate stability threshold, including loss recovery, sharpness behavior, and divergence.
Whether batch normalization speeds accuracy gains or permits higher learning rates, and the stated Fixup comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet20
rows.operation_detail: Trained after layerwise magnitude pruning at initialization; training loss plotted by epoch for different pruning rates.
rows.note: The authors state that sparse networks trained from scratch with SGD show a slowdown in training. The plot shows training loss but does not report classification error or precise values in text.
rows.check: The reported pruning-related slowdown is supported, but 'partial' cannot describe any claim version: training loss alone does not establish V1's training classification error. Appendix I.1 specifies SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0001, and learning rate 0.1 reduced to 0.01 after 91 epochs.

rows.subject: 3-layer linear network, hidden width m = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD; training loss tracked during training.

conditions.value: subset of Cifar-10 (n = 1000), downsampled to 3 × 8 × 8 and whitened

rows.uncertainty: Shaded area corresponds to one standard deviation from the mean.
rows.note: The text specifies the training setup and plots loss, but gives no textual loss values or classification-error result.
rows.check: A linear-network training-loss trajectory does not measure any version's effect. The record's associated condition-number finding of 6–12 is a separate measure and should not be presented as the value of this training-loss row.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer feed-forward network with ReLU activation
rows.operation_detail: Compared training loss across hidden widths; networks were trained with SGD at a fixed learning rate selected by grid search.

conditions.value: 0.3 for widths 15 and 20; 0.5 for all remaining widths

rows.note: Authors state that larger width improves convergence speed; the figure plots training loss but does not report classification error.
rows.check: The authors report faster convergence with greater width, but this is not V2's teacher–student spurious-minimum outcome. Width comparisons also use different learning rates: 0.3 for widths 15 and 20, versus 0.5 for larger widths. 'Observed' is therefore inappropriate as a state against these versions.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
